newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch say EMU is cohesive, not divisive.
newsitem.headline: Dutch say EMU is cohesive, not divisive.

text.p: Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm on Thursday dismissed British warnings that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) could split Europe, saying the effect of the single currency plan was cohesive rather than divisive.

British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind warned in a speech in Switzerland last month that EMU could split the European Union into two groups for the foreseeable future because around half of the 15 members would not meet the eligibility criteria.
But Zalm said the EMU convergence process was having a beneficial effect, drawing all EU states closer together, even those unlikely to be among the first to qualify for EMU.

In a lecture honouring Dutch Nobel prize-winning economist Jan Tinbergen, Zalm noted that Britain and Denmark, which both secured an opt-out from EMU, were both nevertheless working hard towards monetary and economic convergence.

Zalm said it was in the best interests of EU members falling outside the core starter group to build credibility by tracking the single currency as closely as possible. This would make them de facto members of a single currency framework, he added.
Zalm also reiterated Dutch support for a "stability pact" to ensure continuing fiscal discipline among EMU members beyond the launch of the single currency.
"It is imperative that under normal circumstances national governments should strive for a structural budgetary position close to balance," he said.
Zalm concluded that there were compelling economic arguments for EU members to cede monetary sovereignty to an independent European central bank.
The minister also called for reform of the EU's agricultural policy and its structural funds, saying the costs would otherwise become unsustainable as the EU admitted new members.
The Netherlands would lobby strongly for major changes in both areas, he said.
"Fundamental changes to spending are not only desirable in themselves but downright indispensable in view of the costs that will otherwise be involved in European expansion," Zalm said.
